pages.title: The shared factual brief
pages.instruction: Read for the facts and the different priorities
pages.author: Event update card · simulated source
pages.subject: Fictional dates: December 2026
paragraphs: This simulated message is prepared on Thursday 3 December 2026. The event is moving from Friday 4 December to Monday 7 December. It will still start at ten in the morning in room two. Organisers need an attendance response by Friday 4 December at five in the afternoon. These are fixed facts for both versions of the task.

The first recipient is a client who needs a concise professional update and a clear requested action. The second is a friend who can receive a more informal message. Neither version should imply that simply reading the update counts as agreement to attend. Do not replace the fixed dates with relative expressions that change when the message is read.

pages.title: What a recipient needs
pages.instruction: Read for the facts and the different priorities
pages.author: Communication review · simulated source
pages.subject: A useful response, not just a polite message
paragraphs: A recipient can understand the new date without understanding what reply is expected. “Please acknowledge” may ask only for confirmation that the message has been read. “Please confirm whether you can attend” requests a different commitment. The wording should match the information the organiser actually needs.

Register can change the opening, degree of distance and length. It should not change the date, location or deadline, or hide the action under elaborate courtesy. The task is to make two natural versions of the same update, then repair one specific ambiguity if the recipient asks. Clear informal language is a valid choice for the appropriate relationship.

pages.title: Acknowledgement is not attendance
pages.instruction: Listen for the new information and decide how to respond
pages.message: Hi, Ana. I’ve read the event update, but I’m not sure what you need from me. When you say “please acknowledge”, do you only want me to confirm I’ve seen the message, or do you need to know whether I can attend on Monday? I can send either, but they aren’t the same commitment. Could you also give the response deadline as a day and time rather than “tomorrow”? I sometimes read messages after the day they were sent. The new date, same ten o’clock start and room two are clear. It’s the requested action that needs clarification, so there’s no need to rewrite every factual detail or make the wording more elaborate
